title: The gurdwaras left behind
hook: a prayer for free access to Nankana Sahib and the gurdwaras across the border

segments.voice: Yesterday: fateh, and your line: feed and protect. Today, one of the newest lines in the Ardas, added within living memory.

On the Indian side of the border in Punjab, near the town of Dera Baba Nanak, there's a viewing platform. For years, people climbed it with binoculars to look across a few miles of fields at a white building on the other side. They couldn't go there. They just looked, sometimes for a long time, and some of them wept. The building was Gurdwara Kartarpur Sahib, where Guru Nanak spent his last years and died. It's in Pakistan now. And every day, all over the world, the Ardas asks for a door to open.
screen: `A PLATFORM AND BINOCULARS.` → `A WHITE BUILDING ACROSS THE FIELDS.` → `KARTARPUR, IN PAKISTAN NOW.`

segments.voice: At Partition, when British India was divided into India and Pakistan, the new border ran straight through Punjab. The violence of that year fell on Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs alike; huge numbers were killed and uprooted on both sides. Sikh families who had lived in western Punjab for generations left everything and moved east. They left behind places at the heart of Sikh history: Nankana Sahib, where Guru Nanak was born; Kartarpur, where he farmed and died; Panja Sahib at Hasan Abdal; Gurdwara Dera Sahib in Lahore, where Guru Arjan was martyred; and many more. After Partition, a new line entered the Ardas. In paraphrase: grant the Khalsa open access to see, serve and care for Sri Nankana Sahib and the other gurdwaras and holy places from which the Panth has been separated. The word for that separation is vichhora, the ache of being parted from someone you love. It's the same word Gurbani uses for the soul parted from God. Look at what it asks. Not ownership. Not conquest. Khulhe darshan deedaar: to see them freely. And sevaa sambhaal: to serve and look after them. For decades, Sikh pilgrims have crossed in groups for the great festivals, with permission from both governments. More recently, a corridor opened that let pilgrims from India walk to Kartarpur Sahib for the day, though whether it is open has depended on relations between the two countries. Some of the people on that viewing platform finally went. The prayer is still said, every day, for the rest.
screen: `PARTITION: A BORDER THROUGH PUNJAB.` · `NANKANA, KARTARPUR, PANJA SAHIB.` · `VICHHORA: THE ACHE OF BEING PARTED.` · `TO SEE AND SERVE, NOT TO OWN.` · then, large: `DOORS LEFT BEHIND.`

segments.voice: If you can, face west, toward Nankana Sahib from Indian Punjab; if not, picture a horizon. Think of a place you can't go back to, a childhood home, a town, a country, and let yourself feel the vichhora, the ache of it, without hurrying it away. If you pray, say Waheguru toward that horizon.
Vichhora, the ache of being parted from a place or person you love: the Ardas asks to see and serve freely the holy places across the border, Nankana Sahib and Kartarpur among them.
Your line: doors left behind. Not to own them: to see them freely, and to serve. Rest well.

howItsDone: Since Partition, the Ardas has asked for open access to Nankana Sahib and the other gurdwaras in Pakistan; Sikh pilgrims cross for major festivals, and the Kartarpur corridor has at times allowed day visits from India.

chat.says: What does the Ardas ask for about Nankana Sahib and Kartarpur?
options: Open access to see, serve and care for the holy places the Panth was parted from.
Nothing: the Ardas was fixed long before Partition, so it never names them.
Only that Sikhs remember them; it doesn't ask to visit or care for them.
chat.meaning: After Partition the Ardas asks for khulhe darshan deedaar and sevaa sambhaal: to see and serve those places freely, not to own them.
